questions.question:
Assertion (A): The probability of getting a bad egg in a lot of 400 is 0.035; the number of good eggs in the lot is 386.
Reason (R): If the probability of an event is p, the probability of its complementary event is 1 - p.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Number of bad eggs = 0.035 x 400 = 14, so good eggs = 400 - 14 = 386, confirming A is true. R correctly states the complementary probability rule, and it directly explains how A's figure of 386 good eggs was derived (using 1 - 0.035 = 0.965 as the probability of a good egg, or equivalently subtracting the 14 bad eggs from 400).

questions.topic: Comparing probabilities of an odd sum versus an odd product with two dice
questions.question: Naima has two identical 6-sided dice, each with 3 even-numbered faces and 3 odd-numbered faces. She rolls both dice simultaneously and wins a prize if either: Option 1, the sum of the two numbers shown is odd; or Option 2, the product of the two numbers shown is odd. Which option should she choose for a higher chance of winning, and why?

rubric.point: The sum is odd only when one die shows odd and the other even (odd+even or even+odd); since each die is odd with probability 1/2, P(sum odd) = 2 x (1/2 x 1/2) = 1/2
The product is odd only when BOTH dice show odd numbers; P(product odd) = 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4
Since 1/2 > 1/4, Naima should choose Option 1 (the sum being odd)

questions.model_answer: With each die equally likely to show an odd or even number, the sum of the two dice is odd only in the cases odd+even or even+odd, giving P(sum odd) = 2 x (1/2 x 1/2) = 1/2. The product of the two dice is odd only when both dice show odd numbers (odd x odd = odd; any even factor makes the product even), giving P(product odd) = 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4. Since 1/2 is greater than 1/4, Naima has a better chance of winning with Option 1 (sum is odd).

questions.topic: Card probability - face cards, aces/kings, and compound conditions
questions.question: One card is drawn from a well-shuffled standard deck of 52 playing cards. Find the probability of getting: (i) a face card or a black card, (ii) neither an ace nor a king, (iii) a card that is both a jack and a black card.

rubric.point: (i) P(face or black) = P(face)+P(black)-P(face and black) = 12/52 + 26/52 - 6/52 = 32/52 = 8/13
(ii) P(neither ace nor king) = 1 - P(ace or king) = 1 - (4/52+4/52) = 1 - 8/52 = 44/52 = 11/13
(iii) There are 2 black jacks (jack of spades, jack of clubs) out of 52 cards, so P = 2/52 = 1/26

questions.model_answer: (i) There are 12 face cards and 26 black cards in a deck, with 6 cards that are both (the black face cards: J,Q,K of spades and clubs). By inclusion-exclusion, P(face or black) = 12/52 + 26/52 - 6/52 = 32/52 = 8/13. (ii) There are 4 aces and 4 kings (no overlap), so P(ace or king) = 8/52. Hence P(neither ace nor king) = 1 - 8/52 = 44/52 = 11/13. (iii) There are exactly 2 jacks that are also black (jack of spades and jack of clubs), so P(jack and black) = 2/52 = 1/26.

chapters.title: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

notes.overview: This chapter covers pairs of linear equations in two variables - two equations of the form ax+by=c that are considered together - including how to represent them graphically, the three algebraic methods for solving them (substitution, elimination and cross-multiplication), and how to translate word problems into a pair of equations and solve them.

sections.title: 1. What is a Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
sections.content: A linear equation in two variables x and y has the general form ax+by+c=0, where a and b are not both zero. A 'pair' of such equations, considered together, is called a system or pair of linear equations in two variables. Solving the pair means finding the value(s) of x and y that satisfy both equations simultaneously.

sections.title: 2. Graphical Representation and Types of Solutions
sections.content: Each linear equation represents a straight line on a graph. Two lines can: (a) intersect at exactly one point - the pair has a unique solution (consistent, independent); (b) coincide (be the same line) - the pair has infinitely many solutions (consistent, dependent); (c) be parallel and never meet - the pair has no solution (inconsistent). Comparing the ratios a1/a2, b1/b2, c1/c2 tells you which case applies without drawing the graph.

sections.title: 3. Consistency Conditions
sections.content: For a1x+b1y+c1=0 and a2x+b2y+c2=0: if a1/a2 != b1/b2, the pair has a unique solution (intersecting lines). If a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2, the pair has infinitely many solutions (coincident lines). If a1/a2 = b1/b2 != c1/c2, the pair has no solution (parallel lines).

sections.title: 4. Solving by Substitution
sections.content: In the substitution method, solve one equation for one variable in terms of the other, then substitute that expression into the second equation to get a single-variable equation. Solve for that variable, then back-substitute to find the other.
keywords: express one variable in terms of the other

sections.title: 5. Solving by Elimination
sections.content: In the elimination method, multiply one or both equations by suitable constants so that the coefficients of one variable become equal (or opposite), then add or subtract the equations to eliminate that variable, leaving a single-variable equation to solve.
keywords: add or subtract to eliminate a variable

sections.title: 6. Solving by Cross-Multiplication
sections.content: For a1x+b1y+c1=0 and a2x+b2y+c2=0, the cross-multiplication method gives x/(b1c2-b2c1) = y/(c1a2-c2a1) = 1/(a1b2-a2b1), from which x and y can be found directly, provided a1b2-a2b1 is not zero.

sections.title: 7. Word Problems - Setting Up the Equations
sections.content: The key skill for word problems is translating the given information into two equations in two unknowns: identify what the two unknowns represent, write one equation per independent piece of given information, then solve using whichever method is fastest for the specific numbers involved. Common contexts include ages, fares/costs with a fixed + variable component, and exam scoring systems (marks for correct/wrong answers).

key_terms.Linear equation in two variables: An equation of the form ax+by+c=0.
key_terms.Consistent pair: A pair of equations that has at least one solution.
key_terms.Inconsistent pair: A pair of equations that has no solution (parallel lines).
key_terms.Dependent pair: A pair with infinitely many solutions (coincident lines).
key_terms.Substitution method: Solving one equation for one variable and substituting into the other.
key_terms.Elimination method: Adding/subtracting scaled equations to eliminate one variable.

important_facts: a1/a2 != b1/b2 -> unique solution (intersecting lines).
a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2 -> infinitely many solutions (coincident lines).
a1/a2 = b1/b2 != c1/c2 -> no solution (parallel lines).
Fixed-charge-plus-rate word problems (fares, bills) translate to x + (rate)y = total.
Always define your two variables clearly in one line before setting up the equations.
exam_tips: For 'fixed charge + per-unit charge' word problems, write the fixed charge as one variable and the rate as the other - this pattern appears very often in board papers (taxi/auto fares, phone bills, etc.).
Check your final answer by substituting back into BOTH original equations, not just the one you solved last.
When asked to classify a pair of equations (unique/infinite/no solution) without solving, just compare the coefficient ratios - it's much faster than solving fully.

questions.question: The pair of equations 2x+3y=7 and 4x+6y=14 has:
questions.explanation: Here a1/a2=2/4=1/2, b1/b2=3/6=1/2, c1/c2=7/14=1/2 - all equal, so the lines coincide, giving infinitely many solutions.

questions.question: The pair of equations x+2y=4 and 2x+4y=6 represents:
questions.explanation: a1/a2=1/2, b1/b2=2/4=1/2 (equal), but c1/c2=4/6=2/3 (different) - so the lines are parallel with no solution.

questions.question: For the pair 3x+2y=5 and kx-y=1 to have a unique solution, k must NOT equal:
questions.explanation: Unique solution requires a1/a2 != b1/b2, i.e. 3/k != 2/(-1) = -2, so k != 3/(-2) = -3/2. At k=-3/2 the pair fails to have a unique solution.

questions.question: The solution of the pair x+y=10 and x-y=4 is:
questions.explanation: Adding both equations: 2x=14, x=7. Substituting: 7+y=10, y=3.

questions.question: If the graphs of a pair of linear equations are two lines that intersect at exactly one point, the pair is:
questions.explanation: Intersecting lines meet at exactly one point, giving a unique solution - this is called a consistent, independent pair.

questions.question: The sum of two numbers is 26 and their difference is 8. If the numbers are x and y (x>y), which pair of equations represents this?
questions.explanation: Directly translating: sum is 26 gives x+y=26; difference is 8 gives x-y=8.

questions.question: To eliminate x from 2x+3y=12 and 4x+5y=22 by elimination, you would multiply the first equation by:
questions.explanation: Multiplying the first equation by 2 gives 4x+6y=24, matching the x-coefficient of the second equation (4x+5y=22) - subtracting the two then eliminates x.

questions.question: For the equations 3x+2y=5 and 6x+4y=k to have no solution, k must be:
questions.explanation: a1/a2=3/6=1/2=b1/b2=2/4. For no solution we need c1/c2 to differ from 1/2, i.e. 5/k != 1/2, so k != 10.

questions.question: Solve the pair of equations 2x+3y=13 and 3x-2y=0 using the elimination method.

rubric.point: Multiply to equalise a coefficient: 2(2x+3y=13)->4x+6y=26; 3(3x-2y=0)->9x-6y=0; add to get 13x=26, x=2

questions.model_answer: Multiplying the first equation by 2: 4x+6y=26. Multiplying the second by 3: 9x-6y=0. Adding: 13x=26, so x=2. Substituting into 3x-2y=0: 6-2y=0, so y=3.

questions.question: Without solving, determine whether the pair 5x-3y=11 and -10x+6y=-22 has a unique solution, no solution, or infinitely many solutions.

rubric.point: Since all three ratios are equal, the pair has infinitely many solutions

questions.model_answer: a1/a2 = 5/-10 = -1/2, b1/b2 = -3/6 = -1/2, c1/c2 = 11/-22 = -1/2. All three ratios are equal, so the pair represents coincident lines with infinitely many solutions.

questions.question: Ten years ago, a father was twelve times as old as his son. Ten years hence, the father will be twice as old as his son. Find their present ages (set up the equations; you don't need to fully solve).

rubric.point: Let present ages be x (father) and y (son)

questions.model_answer: Let the present ages of the father and son be x and y respectively. Ten years ago: x-10 = 12(y-10). Ten years hence: x+10 = 2(y+10). (Solving these gives x=70, y=20.)

questions.topic: Word problem - fixed and variable cost
questions.question: A taxi charges a fixed charge plus a per-km rate. For a journey of 10 km the charge is Rs 105, and for 15 km it is Rs 155. Find the fixed charge and the rate per km.

rubric.point: Let fixed charge = x, rate per km = y; set up x+10y=105, x+15y=155
Substitute to get x=5; state fixed charge Rs 5, rate Rs 10/km

questions.model_answer: Let the fixed charge be Rs x and the rate per km be Rs y. Then x+10y=105 and x+15y=155. Subtracting: 5y=50, so y=10. Substituting: x+100=105, so x=5. The fixed charge is Rs 5 and the rate is Rs 10 per km.

A boat goes 30 km upstream and 44 km downstream in 10 hours. In another trip, it goes 40 km upstream and 55 km downstream in 13 hours. Find the speed of the boat in still water and the speed of the stream.

rubric.point: Let boat speed = x km/h, stream speed = y km/h; upstream speed=(x-y), downstream=(x+y)
Solve the linear pair in u,v to get u=1/5, v=1/11 (so x-y=5, x+y=11)
Solve for x and y: x=8 km/h, y=3 km/h

questions.model_answer: Let the boat's speed in still water be x km/h and the stream's speed be y km/h, so upstream speed = x-y and downstream speed = x+y. From the two trips: 30/(x-y)+44/(x+y)=10 and 40/(x-y)+55/(x+y)=13. Substituting u=1/(x-y) and v=1/(x+y): 30u+44v=10 and 40u+55v=13. Solving this pair (by elimination) gives u=1/5 and v=1/11, so x-y=5 and x+y=11. Adding: 2x=16, x=8. Subtracting: 2y=6, y=3. The boat's speed in still water is 8 km/h and the stream's speed is 3 km/h.

questions.topic: Case study - exam scoring system (adapted from CBSE Question Bank)
questions.passage: A test consists of 'True' or 'False' questions. One mark is awarded for every correct answer, while 1/4 mark is deducted for every wrong answer. A student answered all 120 questions in the test - some he knew the answer to, and the rest he attempted by guessing. Assume every question he attempted by guessing turned out to be wrong. He scored 90 marks in total.

subquestions.question: How many questions did he answer correctly?

subquestions.model_answer: If he answered 80 correctly out of 120, the remaining 40 were guessed and wrong. Score = 80x1 - 40x0.25 = 80 - 10 = 70 marks.

Assertion (A): The pair of equations x-2y=0 and 3x+4y-20=0 has a unique solution.
Reason (R): For a1x+b1y=c1 and a2x+b2y=c2, a unique solution exists when a1/a2 != b1/b2.

Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.

Reason (R): If a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2, the lines coincide, giving infinitely many solutions, not zero.

Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.question: Solve the pair 2x+y=5 and 3x+2y=8.

questions.question: A two-digit number has digits summing to 9. If 27 is subtracted from the number, the digits reverse. Find the number.

rubric.point: Let tens digit=x, units digit=y; x+y=9

questions.model_answer: Let the tens digit be x and units digit be y, so x+y=9. The number is 10x+y; reversed it is 10y+x. Given (10x+y)-27=10y+x: 9x-9y=27, so x-y=3. Solving x+y=9 and x-y=3: x=6, y=3. The number is 63 (check: 63-27=36, which is 63 with digits reversed).

questions.question: 5 years ago, A's age was 3 times B's age. 10 years hence, A will be twice as old as B. Find their present ages.

rubric.point: Simplify both to A=3B-10 and A=2B+10

questions.model_answer: (A-5)=3(B-5) simplifies to A=3B-10. (A+10)=2(B+10) simplifies to A=2B+10. Setting equal: 3B-10=2B+10, so B=20, and A=2(20)+10=50.

questions.question: Solve the pair 3x+2y=11 and 2x+3y=4.
questions.model_answer: Multiplying the first by 3 and second by 2: 9x+6y=33 and 4x+6y=8. Subtracting: 5x=25, so x=5. Substituting into 3x+2y=11: 15+2y=11, so y=-2.

questions.question: A fraction becomes 9/11 if 2 is added to both numerator and denominator, and 5/6 if 3 is added to both. Find the fraction.

rubric.point: Set up 11(x+2)=9(y+2) and 6(x+3)=5(y+3), simplifying to 11x-9y=-4 and 6x-5y=-3

questions.model_answer: (x+2)/(y+2)=9/11 gives 11x-9y=-4. (x+3)/(y+3)=5/6 gives 6x-5y=-3. Solving these simultaneously: x=7, y=9. The fraction is 7/9.

questions.question: 10 years ago, a father's age was thrice his son's age. 10 years hence, the father's age will be twice his son's age. Find their present ages.
questions.model_answer: Let present ages be f (father) and s (son). 10 years ago: f-10=3(s-10), so f=3s-20. 10 years hence: f+10=2(s+10), so f=2s+10. Setting equal: 3s-20=2s+10, giving s=30. Then f=2(30)+10=70. The father is 70 and the son is 30.

questions.topic: Condition for a pair of linear equations to have a determinable solution type
questions.question:
Two linear equations are given as a1x + b1y + c = 0 and a2x + b2y + c = 0 (note both share the same constant term c). Which single piece of information is, by itself, sufficient to determine whether a solution exists?
I. a1/b1 = a2/b2 = 1
II. a1/a2 = b1/b2
III. a1/a2 = b1/b2 != 1
IV. a1/a2 != b1/b2
questions.explanation: Since both equations share the same constant c, the ratio c1/c2 = 1 always. Condition I (a1/b1=a2/b2=1) actually forces a1=b1 and a2=b2, which combined with equal c makes both lines identical (a valid, if very specific, determination that infinite solutions exist). Condition IV directly says a1/a2 != b1/b2, which by itself guarantees the lines intersect at a unique point regardless of c - both I and IV are each independently sufficient to settle the question, matching the official answer.

questions.topic: Forming linear equations from a circular-track walking problem
questions.question: Kimaya and Heena start walking from the same point P at the same time in opposite directions on an 800 m circular path. Kimaya walks to the clubhouse at 100 m/min and Heena walks to the badminton court at 80 m/min. The distance along the track between the clubhouse and the badminton court (the short way) is 180 m. If Heena takes 1 minute more than Kimaya to reach her destination, find the time taken by Heena.

rubric.point: Let Kimaya's time be t1 and Heena's time be t2, so t2 - t1 = 1, and since they walk in opposite directions around an 800 m loop with 180 m between their destinations, the sum of distances covered is 800 - 180 = 620 m
Setting up 100t1 + 80t2 = 620 and substituting t1 = t2 - 1 gives 100(t2-1) + 80t2 = 620, which solves to t2 = 4 minutes

questions.model_answer: Let the time taken by Kimaya be t1 minutes and by Heena be t2 minutes, so t2 - t1 = 1. Since they walk in opposite directions around the 800 m circular path and end up 180 m apart (the gap between the clubhouse and badminton court), the distances they've covered together add up to 800 - 180 = 620 m: 100t1 + 80t2 = 620. Substituting t1 = t2 - 1: 100(t2 - 1) + 80t2 = 620, i.e. 180t2 - 100 = 620, so t2 = 4. Heena takes 4 minutes to reach the badminton court.

questions.topic: Finding values of m and n for unique, infinite, or no solutions
questions.question: For the pair of linear equations 2x - my = 9 and 4x - ny = 9, find at least one pair of possible values of m and n (if they exist) for which the pair has: (i) a unique solution, (ii) infinitely many solutions, (iii) no solution.

rubric.point: (i) For a unique solution, need a1/a2 != b1/b2, i.e. 2/4 != -m/-n; any m, n not satisfying m/n=1/2 works, e.g. m=2, n=6 (giving 2x-2y=9, 4x-6y=9)

(ii) For infinitely many solutions, need a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2, i.e. 2/4 = m/n = 9/9 = 1; but 2/4 = 1/2 != 1, so this condition can never be satisfied - infinitely many solutions is not achievable for any m, n here

(iii) For no solution, need a1/a2 = b1/b2 != c1/c2; since c1=c2=9 always gives c1/c2=1, choose m, n with m/n = 1/2 (matching the fixed a1/a2 ratio, which is automatically != 1), e.g. m=3, n=6 (giving 2x-3y=9, 4x-6y=9)

questions.model_answer: In general, for a1x+b1y=c1 and a2x+b2y=c2: a unique solution needs a1/a2 != b1/b2; infinitely many solutions needs a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2; no solution needs a1/a2 = b1/b2 != c1/c2. Here a1/a2 = 2/4 = 1/2 is fixed, and since both constants equal 9, c1/c2 = 1 is also fixed. (i) Unique solution: choose any m, n with -m/-n != 1/2, e.g. m=2, n=6, giving 2x-2y=9 and 4x-6y=9 (here m/n=1/3 != 1/2). (ii) Infinitely many solutions would require m/n = 1/2 = c1/c2 = 1, which is impossible since 1/2 != 1 - so no choice of m, n can give infinitely many solutions for this pair. (iii) No solution: choose m, n with m/n = 1/2 (matching a1/a2) but obviously != c1/c2=1, e.g. m=3, n=6, giving 2x-3y=9 and 4x-6y=9.

questions.topic: Word problem - forming and solving a pair of linear equations for rectangle dimensions
questions.question: The area of a rectangle reduces by 160 sq. m if its length is increased by 5 m and breadth is reduced by 4 m. However, if the length is decreased by 10 m and the breadth is increased by 2 m, the area decreases by 100 sq. m. Find the dimensions of the rectangle.

rubric.point: Let length = x, breadth = y. First condition: (x+5)(y-4) = xy - 160; expanding gives xy - 4x + 5y - 20 = xy - 160, which simplifies to 4x - 5y = 140
Second condition: (x-10)(y+2) = xy - 100, expanding gives xy+2x-10y-20=xy-100, i.e. 2x-10y=-80, i.e. x-5y=-40
Solving the two equations simultaneously (e.g. subtracting) gives x = 60 m and y = 20 m

questions.model_answer: Let the length be x m and breadth y m. From the first condition, (x+5)(y-4) = xy - 160. Expanding: xy - 4x + 5y - 20 = xy - 160, which simplifies to 4x - 5y = 140. From the second condition, (x-10)(y+2) = xy - 100. Expanding: xy + 2x - 10y - 20 = xy - 100, which simplifies to 2x - 10y = -80, i.e. x - 5y = -40. Multiplying this by 4: 4x - 20y = -160. Subtracting from the first equation (4x - 5y = 140): 15y = 300, so y = 20. Substituting back: x - 5(20) = -40, so x = 60. The rectangle is 60 m long and 20 m wide.

notes.overview: This chapter uses algebra to study geometry on the Cartesian plane: finding the distance between two points, finding the coordinates of a point that divides a line segment in a given ratio (the section formula), and finding the area of a triangle given the coordinates of its vertices.

sections.title: 1. The Distance Formula
sections.content: The distance between two points A(x1,y1) and B(x2,y2) is given by AB = sqrt((x2-x1)^2 + (y2-y1)^2). This comes directly from the Pythagoras theorem applied to the horizontal and vertical differences between the two points.

sections.title: 2. Distance from the Origin
sections.content: The distance of a point P(x,y) from the origin O(0,0) is a special case of the distance formula: OP = sqrt(x^2+y^2).

sections.title: 3. The Section Formula
sections.content: If a point P(x,y) divides the line segment joining A(x1,y1) and B(x2,y2) internally in the ratio m:n, then P = ((mx2+nx1)/(m+n), (my2+ny1)/(m+n)). This is used to find a point at a specified fraction of the way along a segment, not just the midpoint.

sections.title: 4. The Midpoint Formula
sections.content: The midpoint of the segment joining A(x1,y1) and B(x2,y2) is a special case of the section formula with ratio 1:1: midpoint = ((x1+x2)/2, (y1+y2)/2).
keywords: special case of section formula, ratio 1:1

sections.title: 5. Area of a Triangle from Coordinates
sections.content: The area of a triangle with vertices (x1,y1), (x2,y2), (x3,y3) is (1/2)|x1(y2-y3) + x2(y3-y1) + x3(y1-y2)|. If this expression evaluates to 0, the three points are collinear (they lie on a single straight line, so no triangle is formed).

sections.title: 6. Collinearity of Points
sections.content: Three points are collinear if the area of the 'triangle' they form works out to exactly 0 using the area formula. This gives an algebraic way to check collinearity without needing to plot the points.

sections.title: 7. Applying These Formulas to Word Problems
sections.content: Many real-world problems (marking out points on a sports field, dividing a garden plot, positioning flags at fractional distances) translate directly into distance, section-formula, or area calculations once the relevant points are identified and assigned coordinates based on the given description.

key_terms.Section formula: The formula giving the coordinates of a point dividing a segment in a given ratio m:n.
key_terms.Midpoint formula: The special case of the section formula for ratio 1:1.
key_terms.Collinear points: Points that lie on the same straight line (triangle area = 0).

important_facts: Distance formula: AB = sqrt((x2-x1)^2+(y2-y1)^2).
Section formula (ratio m:n): P = ((mx2+nx1)/(m+n), (my2+ny1)/(m+n)).
Midpoint formula: ((x1+x2)/2, (y1+y2)/2).
Area of a triangle: (1/2)|x1(y2-y3)+x2(y3-y1)+x3(y1-y2)|.
Three points are collinear exactly when this area works out to 0.
exam_tips: Always take the absolute value (modulus) of the area expression before finalising your answer - area cannot be negative, and forgetting this is a common way marks are lost.

When a question says 'divides in the ratio m:n', double check whether it's asking for the point closer to the first or second named point - the formula depends on which point is 'first' (x1,y1) and which is 'second' (x2,y2).
For collinearity questions, it is usually faster to compute the area expression directly and check if it's 0, rather than trying to compare slopes.

questions.topic: Comprehensive - point equidistant from two points
questions.question: Find the point on the y-axis which is equidistant from the points (5,-2) and (-3,2), showing full working.
questions.model_answer: Let the point be (0,y). Setting distances equal: sqrt(25+(y+2)^2) = sqrt(9+(y-2)^2). Squaring: 25+(y+2)^2 = 9+(y-2)^2. Expanding: 25+y^2+4y+4 = 9+y^2-4y+4. Simplifying: 25+4y = 9-4y+0... collecting terms: 8y = 9-25-4+4, giving 8y=-16, so y=-2. The point is (0,-2).

questions.question: The points D(1,1), E(2,-3) and F(3,4) are the midpoints of sides BC, CA and AB respectively of a triangle ABC. Find the coordinates of A, B and C.

rubric.point: Set up the relationships: A+B=2F, B+C=2D, C+A=2E
Solve the resulting linear system for the x-coordinates

questions.model_answer: Since D,E,F are midpoints: A+B=2F=(6,8), B+C=2D=(2,2), C+A=2E=(4,-6). Adding all three: 2(A+B+C)=(12,4), so A+B+C=(6,2). Subtracting each pairwise sum: A=(6,2)-(2,2)=(4,0), B=(6,2)-(4,-6)=(2,8), C=(6,2)-(6,8)=(0,-6).

questions.topic: Points equidistant from two given points - assertion and reason
questions.question:
P(-2, 5) and Q(2, -1) are two points on the coordinate plane.
Assertion (A): The midpoint (0, 2) is the only point equidistant from P and Q.
Reason (R): There are many points (x, y) satisfying (x+2)^2 + (y-5)^2 = (x-2)^2 + (y+1)^2 that are equidistant from P and Q.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: A is false: the set of points equidistant from P and Q is not just the midpoint but the entire perpendicular bisector line of segment PQ - infinitely many points satisfy this. R is true: the given equation (equating squared distances to P and Q) is exactly the equation of that perpendicular bisector line, which indeed has many solutions (x,y), all equidistant from P and Q.

questions.topic: Finding possible coordinates using the distance formula
questions.question: The distance between two points A and B is given as sqrt(10^2 + 7^2). The coordinates of A are (-4, 3), and B lies in the first quadrant. What can be said of all possible x-coordinates of point B?
questions.explanation: Matching the distance formula sqrt((x+4)^2+(y-3)^2) = sqrt(10^2+7^2), the differences 10 and 7 can be assigned (with sign) to (x+4) and (y-3) in either order. For B in the first quadrant (x>0, y>0): x+4 = 10 gives x=6, or x+4=7 gives x=3 (x+4=-10 or -7 give negative x, rejected). Both 6 and 3 are multiples of 3.

questions.topic: Finding the fourth vertex of a parallelogram using the midpoint of diagonals
questions.question: A(1,2), B(4,3) and C(6,6) are three vertices of a parallelogram ABCD. What are the coordinates of the fourth vertex D?
questions.explanation: In parallelogram ABCD, the diagonals AC and BD bisect each other. Midpoint of AC = ((1+6)/2, (2+6)/2) = (3.5, 4). Setting this equal to the midpoint of BD: ((4+x)/2, (3+y)/2) = (3.5, 4) gives x = 3, y = 5. So D = (3, 5).

notes.overview: This chapter studies tangents to a circle - lines that touch the circle at exactly one point - and the key theorems governing their behaviour, along with the important idea of tangent lengths from an external point, which is frequently used in case-study problems involving a circle inscribed in a triangle or polygon.

sections.title: 1. Tangent to a Circle
sections.content: A tangent to a circle is a line that touches the circle at exactly one point (the point of contact), and does not cross into the circle's interior at any other point. A secant, by contrast, intersects the circle at two points.

sections.title: 2. Tangent Perpendicular to the Radius
sections.content: The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius drawn to that point of contact. This is the single most-used fact in this chapter's proofs and numerical problems.
keywords: tangent perpendicular to radius at point of contact

sections.title: 3. Number of Tangents from a Point
sections.content: From a point inside the circle, no tangent can be drawn. From a point on the circle, exactly one tangent can be drawn (at that point). From a point outside the circle, exactly two tangents can be drawn.

sections.title: 4. Equal Tangent Lengths from an External Point
sections.content: The lengths of the two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal. This is proved using the congruence of the two right triangles formed by the external point, each point of contact, and the centre (both have the same hypotenuse, one leg equal to the radius, and a right angle at the point of contact).
keywords: tangent lengths from an external point are equal

sections.title: 5. Tangent Lengths and the Incircle of a Triangle
sections.content: When a circle is inscribed in a triangle (touching all three sides), the tangent lengths from each vertex to the two adjacent points of contact are equal. If the incircle touches AB, BC, CA at D, E, F, then AD=AF, BD=BE, CE=CF, and each of these can be found using the semi-perimeter: AD = s - BC, BE = s - CA, CF = s - AB (where s is the semi-perimeter).

sections.title: 6. Area of a Triangle Using its Inradius
sections.content: If a circle of radius r is inscribed in a triangle with semi-perimeter s, the area of the triangle equals r x s. This is a quick way to relate a triangle's area, its perimeter and its inscribed circle's radius.
keywords: Area = r x s (inradius x semi-perimeter)

key_terms.Tangent: A line touching a circle at exactly one point.
key_terms.Secant: A line intersecting a circle at two points.
key_terms.Point of contact: The single point where a tangent touches the circle.
key_terms.Incircle: A circle inscribed inside a triangle, touching all three sides.
key_terms.Inradius: The radius of a triangle's incircle.
key_terms.Semi-perimeter: Half the perimeter of a triangle, denoted s.

important_facts: The tangent at a point is perpendicular to the radius at that point.
Exactly two tangents can be drawn from an external point, and they are equal in length.
For a triangle's incircle touching AB, BC, CA at D, E, F: AD=AF=s-BC, BE=BD=s-CA, CF=CE=s-AB.
Area of a triangle = inradius x semi-perimeter (r x s).
No tangent can be drawn from a point inside the circle.
exam_tips: Whenever you see 'tangent' and 'radius' together in a problem, immediately look for a right angle at the point of contact - it's almost always the key to the solution.
For incircle/tangent-length problems, write out AD=AF, BD=BE, CE=CF as a first step - most of these problems become simple simultaneous equations once you do.
Remember Area = r x s for a triangle with an inscribed circle - it often provides a fast shortcut compared to Heron's formula.

questions.question: The tangent to a circle at a point is always:
options: parallel to the radius at that point
perpendicular to the radius at that point
equal in length to the radius
questions.explanation: A fundamental property: the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius drawn to that point of contact.

questions.question: The number of tangents that can be drawn from a point outside a circle is:
questions.explanation: Exactly two tangents can be drawn from any point lying outside a circle.

questions.question: If the length of a tangent from a point P, 25 cm away from the centre of a circle, is 24 cm, the radius of the circle is:
questions.explanation: By Pythagoras (right angle at point of contact): r^2 = 25^2 - 24^2 = 625-576 = 49, so r=7 cm.

questions.question: PA and PB are tangents drawn from an external point P to a circle with centre O. If angle APB = 60 degrees, then angle AOB is:
questions.explanation: OAPB forms a quadrilateral with right angles at A and B (tangent-radius property); angles sum to 360, so angle AOB = 360-90-90-60 = 120 degrees.

questions.question: A circle is inscribed in triangle ABC touching sides AB, BC, CA at D, E, F. If AB=10, BC=8, CA=6, then AD equals:
questions.explanation: Semi-perimeter s = (10+8+6)/2 = 12. AD = s - BC = 12-8 = 4.

questions.question: How many tangents can be drawn from a point lying inside a circle?
questions.explanation: No tangent can be drawn from a point inside a circle, since any line through an interior point must cross the circle at two points (it's a secant, not a tangent).

questions.question: A point P is at a distance of 13 cm from the centre O of a circle of radius 5 cm. Find the length of the tangent drawn from P to the circle.

rubric.point: Recognise the right angle at the point of contact, apply Pythagoras: PT^2 = PO^2 - OT^2

questions.model_answer: Since the tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact T, triangle OTP is right-angled at T. PT = sqrt(PO^2 - OT^2) = sqrt(13^2-5^2) = sqrt(169-25) = sqrt(144) = 12 cm.

questions.question: Two tangents PA and PB are drawn from an external point P to a circle with centre O, such that angle AOB = 130 degrees. Find angle APB.

rubric.point: Recognise OAPB is a quadrilateral with right angles at A and B
keywords: right angles at A and B

rubric.point: Sum of angles = 360: angle APB = 360-90-90-130 = 50 degrees

questions.model_answer: In quadrilateral OAPB, angles at A and B are 90 degrees each (tangent perpendicular to radius). Sum of all four angles = 360 degrees, so angle APB = 360 - 90 - 90 - 130 = 50 degrees.

questions.question: A circle touches all three sides of triangle ABC, with AB=12 cm, BC=8 cm and CA=10 cm. Find the lengths AD, BE and CF, where D, E, F are the points of contact on AB, BC and CA respectively.
questions.model_answer: Semi-perimeter s = (12+8+10)/2 = 15. AD = s-BC = 15-8 = 7 cm. BE = s-CA = 15-10 = 5 cm. CF = s-AB = 15-12 = 3 cm.

questions.question: From an external point P, two tangents PA and PB are drawn to a circle with centre O and radius 6 cm. If PO=10 cm, find the length of PA and the area of quadrilateral OAPB.

rubric.point: Area of OAPB = 2 x area of triangle OAP = 2 x (1/2 x OA x PA)
Area = 2 x (1/2 x 6 x 8) = 48 sq cm

questions.model_answer: PA = sqrt(PO^2-OA^2) = sqrt(10^2-6^2) = sqrt(100-36) = sqrt(64) = 8 cm. Since PB=PA=8 cm (equal tangents) and triangles OAP, OBP are congruent right triangles, area of OAPB = 2 x area of triangle OAP = 2 x (1/2 x 6 x 8) = 2 x 24 = 48 sq cm.

questions.question: (a) Prove that the lengths of the two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal. (b) Using this result, if a quadrilateral ABCD is drawn to circumscribe a circle, prove that AB+CD = BC+AD.

rubric.point: (a) Draw OA, OB, OP; note angle OAP=angle OBP=90 (tangent-radius), OA=OB (radii), OP common
(a) Triangles OAP and OBP are congruent (RHS), so PA=PB
(b) Let the circle touch AB,BC,CD,DA at P,Q,R,S; use equal tangent lengths from each vertex: AP=AS, BP=BQ, CQ=CR, DR=DS

questions.model_answer: (a) Let PA and PB be two tangents from external point P to a circle with centre O, touching at A and B. In triangles OAP and OBP: OA=OB (radii), OP=OP (common), angle OAP=angle OBP=90 degrees (tangent perpendicular to radius). By RHS congruence, triangle OAP is congruent to triangle OBP, so PA=PB. (b) Let the incircle of quadrilateral ABCD touch AB, BC, CD, DA at P, Q, R, S respectively. By the result in (a): AP=AS, BP=BQ, CQ=CR, DR=DS. Adding: AB+CD = (AP+PB)+(CR+RD) = (AS+BQ)+(CQ+DS) = (AS+DS)+(BQ+CQ) = AD+BC. Hence AB+CD = BC+AD.

questions.passage: Varun designed a logo for his school's Sports Day T-shirts. The logo is a circle with centre O inscribed in a triangle ABC, touching sides AB, BC and CA at points D, E and F respectively. The lengths of sides AB, BC and CA are 12 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm respectively.

subquestions.question: What is the length of AD?
subquestions.explanation: Semi-perimeter s = (12+8+10)/2 = 15. AD = s-BC = 15-8 = 7 cm.

rubric.point: Use Area = r x s, with r=4, s=15

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A tangent to a circle can also pass through the centre of the circle.
Reason (R): The tangent at a point is always perpendicular to the radius at that point.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: A is false - a tangent can never pass through the centre, since it must be perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, and a line through the centre along the radius direction would be the radius itself, not perpendicular to it. R is a true, correctly stated property.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): If PA and PB are tangents from an external point P to a circle, then PA=PB.
Reason (R): Triangles OAP and OBP are congruent by the RHS congruence rule.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: A is true (a standard, provable result). R correctly identifies the RHS congruence argument used to prove it, and correctly explains A.

questions.question: The angle between a tangent to a circle and the radius drawn to the point of contact is:
questions.explanation: The tangent is always perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.

questions.question: A tangent from a point 25 cm from the centre of a circle has length 24 cm. The radius of the circle is:
questions.explanation: By Pythagoras: r=sqrt(25^2-24^2)=sqrt(625-576)=sqrt(49)=7 cm.

questions.topic: Chord tangent to a smaller concentric circle
questions.question: Two concentric circles have radii 13 cm and 5 cm. The length of a chord of the larger circle that is tangent to the smaller circle is:
questions.explanation: Half the chord = sqrt(13^2-5^2)=sqrt(169-25)=12, so the full chord = 24 cm.

questions.question: The number of common tangents that can be drawn to two circles touching each other externally is:
questions.explanation: Two circles touching externally have exactly 3 common tangents (2 direct + 1 at the point of contact).

questions.topic: Common tangents - one circle inside another
questions.question: The number of common tangents to two circles, one lying completely inside the other without touching, is:
questions.explanation: If one circle is entirely inside another without touching, no common tangent can be drawn to both.

questions.question: A tangent from a point 10 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 6 cm has length:
questions.explanation: Tangent length = sqrt(10^2-6^2) = sqrt(64) = 8 cm.

questions.question: If PA and PB are tangents from an external point P, and PA=5cm, then PB equals:
questions.explanation: Tangents from the same external point are always equal in length, so PB=PA=5cm.

questions.question: A circle is inscribed in a triangle with perimeter 30 cm, touching the sides at D, E, F. The sum AD+BE+CF equals:
questions.explanation: AD+BE+CF always equals the semi-perimeter, s = 30/2 = 15 cm.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about a tangent to a circle?
options: It always passes through the centre
It intersects the circle at two points
It touches the circle at exactly one point
It can never touch the circle
questions.explanation: By definition, a tangent touches a circle at exactly one point, and never passes through the centre.

questions.topic: Tangent from a point on the circle
questions.question: How many tangents can be drawn from a point lying exactly on the circle?
questions.explanation: Exactly one tangent can be drawn at a point that lies on the circle itself.

questions.question: If a line is perpendicular to the radius of a circle at the point where the radius meets the circle, that line must be:
questions.explanation: A line perpendicular to the radius at the point where it meets the circle is, by definition, the tangent at that point.

questions.question: From a point 17 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 8 cm, the length of the tangent is:
questions.explanation: Tangent length = sqrt(17^2-8^2) = sqrt(289-64) = sqrt(225) = 15 cm.

questions.question: A point P is 15 cm from the centre O of a circle of radius 9 cm. Find the length of the tangent from P to the circle.
Two tangents PA and PB are drawn from external point P with angle APB = 80 degrees. Find angle AOB.

rubric.point: Recognise OAPB has right angles at A and B

questions.model_answer: In quadrilateral OAPB, angles at A and B are 90 degrees each. Sum of angles = 360, so angle AOB = 360-90-90-80 = 100 degrees.

questions.question: Two concentric circles have radii 13 cm and 5 cm. Find the length of a chord of the larger circle that touches the smaller circle.
questions.model_answer: Half the chord = sqrt(13^2-5^2) = sqrt(169-25) = sqrt(144) = 12 cm, so the full chord length = 24 cm.

questions.question: A circle is inscribed in triangle ABC with AB=7cm, BC=8cm, CA=9cm, touching AB at D. Find the length AD.
questions.model_answer: Semi-perimeter s=(7+8+9)/2=12. AD=s-BC=12-8=4 cm.

questions.question: From an external point P, a tangent PA=12cm is drawn to a circle of radius 5cm. Find the distance OP from P to the centre O.
A quadrilateral ABCD circumscribes a circle, with AB=6cm, BC=9cm and CD=8cm. Find the length AD.

rubric.point: Use AB+CD=BC+AD (equal tangent lengths from each vertex)

questions.model_answer: For a quadrilateral circumscribing a circle, AB+CD=BC+AD. Substituting: 6+8=9+AD, so 14=9+AD, giving AD=5 cm.

questions.question: A circle is inscribed in a triangle with sides AB=15cm, BC=13cm and CA=14cm. Find the tangent lengths AD, BE and CF.
A tangent of length 24 cm is drawn from a point 26 cm away from the centre of a circle. Find the radius of the circle.

questions.topic: Tangent length using OP and radius
questions.question: From an external point P, OP=17cm where O is the centre of a circle of radius 8cm. Find the length of the tangent PA from P.
A triangle inscribed with a circle has area 84 sq cm and perimeter 42 cm. Find the radius of the inscribed circle.

rubric.point: Recall Area = r x s, where s is the semi-perimeter

questions.model_answer: Area = r x s, where s = perimeter/2 = 42/2 = 21. So r = Area/s = 84/21 = 4 cm.

questions.question: A circle is inscribed in a triangle with sides AB=15cm, BC=13cm and CA=14cm, touching them at D, E, F respectively. Find (a) the tangent lengths AD, BE, CF, (b) the area of the triangle (using Heron's formula), (c) the radius of the incircle, and (d) the area of triangle OAB, where O is the centre.

rubric.point: (d) Area of OAB = (1/2) x AB x r = (1/2)x15x4 = 30 sq cm

questions.model_answer: (a) s=(15+13+14)/2=21. AD=s-BC=8cm, BE=s-CA=7cm, CF=s-AB=6cm. (b) By Heron's formula: Area = sqrt(s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)) = sqrt(21x6x7x8) = sqrt(7056) = 84 sq cm. (c) r = Area/s = 84/21 = 4 cm. (d) Area of triangle OAB = (1/2) x AB x r (since the height from O to AB is the inradius) = (1/2) x 15 x 4 = 30 sq cm.

questions.question: From a point P, 25 cm from the centre O of a circle of radius 7 cm, two tangents PA and PB are drawn. Find (a) the length of PA, (b) the length of PB, (c) the area of quadrilateral OAPB.

rubric.point: (b) PB=PA=24cm (equal tangents from an external point)
(c) Area OAPB = 2 x area of OAP = 2 x (1/2 x OA x PA)

questions.model_answer: (a) PA = sqrt(OP^2-OA^2) = sqrt(25^2-7^2) = sqrt(625-49) = sqrt(576) = 24 cm. (b) By the equal-tangent-lengths property, PB=PA=24cm. (c) Since triangles OAP and OBP are congruent right triangles, area of OAPB = 2 x (1/2 x OA x PA) = OA x PA = 7 x 24 = 168 sq cm.

questions.topic: Tangent length using a right triangle formed by the radius and tangent
questions.question: AT is a tangent to a circle with centre O, where OT = 4 cm and angle OTA = 30 degrees. What is the length of AT?
questions.explanation: Since OA (the radius to the point of tangency A) is perpendicular to the tangent line, triangle OAT is right-angled at A, with hypotenuse OT = 4 cm and angle at T = 30 degrees. AT (adjacent to the 30 degree angle) = OT x cos(30) = 4 x (sqrt(3)/2) = 2*sqrt(3) cm.

questions.topic: Radius of a circle inscribed in a quadrilateral with a right angle
questions.question: A circle is inscribed in quadrilateral ABCD, touching AB at P, BC at Q, CD at R and DA at S, with angle B = 90 degrees. If AD = 23 cm, AB = 29 cm and DS = 5 cm, find the radius of the circle.

rubric.point: Since tangents from an external point are equal in length: DS = DR = 5 cm, so AS = AD - DS = 23 - 5 = 18 cm, and AP = AS = 18 cm (tangents from A)
So BP = AB - AP = 29 - 18 = 11 cm; since angle B = 90 degrees and the radii OP, OQ are each perpendicular to the tangents at P and Q, OPBQ is a square, so the radius = BP = 11 cm

questions.model_answer: Tangent segments from the same external point to a circle are equal in length. From D: DS = DR = 5 cm, so AS = AD - DS = 23 - 5 = 18 cm. From A: AP = AS = 18 cm (tangents from A). So BP = AB - AP = 29 - 18 = 11 cm. Since angle B = 90 degrees, and the radii to the points of tangency P (on AB) and Q (on BC) are each perpendicular to their tangent lines, the quadrilateral formed by O, P, B, Q has three right angles (at P, B and Q) and OP = OQ (both radii) - so OPBQ is a square, meaning the radius equals BP = 11 cm.

questions.topic: Proving the tangent-chord angle relationship at an external point
questions.question: Two tangents TP and TQ are drawn to a circle with centre O from an external point T. Prove that angle PTQ = 2 x angle OPQ.

rubric.point: Let angle PTQ = theta. Since TP = TQ (tangents from an external point are equal), triangle TPQ is isosceles, so angle TPQ = angle TQP = 90 - theta/2
Since OP is perpendicular to the tangent TP (radius perpendicular to tangent at point of contact), angle OPT = 90 degrees, so angle OPQ = angle OPT - angle TPQ = 90 - (90 - theta/2) = theta/2
So angle OPQ = theta/2 = (1/2) angle PTQ, i.e. angle PTQ = 2 x angle OPQ, as required

questions.model_answer: Let angle PTQ = theta. Since TP and TQ are tangents from the same external point T, TP = TQ, so triangle TPQ is isosceles, giving angle TPQ = angle TQP = (180 - theta)/2 = 90 - theta/2. Since the radius OP is perpendicular to the tangent TP at the point of contact P, angle OPT = 90 degrees. Therefore angle OPQ = angle OPT - angle TPQ = 90 - (90 - theta/2) = theta/2. This gives angle OPQ = theta/2 = (1/2) angle PTQ, i.e. angle PTQ = 2 x angle OPQ, as required.

notes.overview: This chapter builds on the basic formulas for the circumference and area of a circle to cover areas and perimeters of sectors and segments, and combinations of circles with other plane figures (squares, triangles, and multiple circles arranged together) - a very common source of case-study/real-world questions in board exams.

sections.title: 1. Circumference and Area of a Circle
sections.content: For a circle of radius r: circumference = 2*pi*r, and area = pi*r^2. These are the two most basic formulas the whole chapter builds on.

sections.title: 2. Area and Perimeter of a Sector
sections.content: A sector is the region enclosed by two radii and the arc between them. For a sector with angle theta (in degrees) at the centre of a circle of radius r: area of sector = (theta/360) * pi*r^2, and length of the arc = (theta/360) * 2*pi*r. The perimeter of the sector = arc length + 2r (the two straight radii).

sections.title: 3. Area of a Segment
sections.content: A segment is the region between a chord and the arc it cuts off. Area of a minor segment = area of the corresponding sector - area of the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord.
keywords: segment area = sector area - triangle area

sections.title: 4. Combinations of Circles with Other Figures
sections.content: Many problems combine circles with squares, triangles, or other circles - for example, a circle inscribed in a square, an equilateral triangle inscribed in a circle, or several circles arranged inside a square. The general strategy is to find the area of the outer figure and the area(s) of the circle(s)/other shape(s), then add or subtract as needed to find the 'remaining' or 'shaded' region.
keywords: remaining area = outer figure area - inner figure area(s)

sections.title: 5. Equilateral Triangle Inscribed in a Circle
sections.content: For an equilateral triangle inscribed in a circle of radius R, the side of the triangle is R*sqrt(3), and its height (altitude) is (3/2)*R. These are useful standalone results worth memorising for case-study problems involving circles and inscribed equilateral triangles.

sections.title: 6. Circumference and Area in Real-World 'Wire' and 'Revolution' Problems
sections.content: For problems about wire used to trace a shape (like sectors of a circle divided by diameters), the total wire length is the sum of all straight and curved parts drawn. For 'rolling'/'revolution' problems, the distance covered in one revolution equals the circumference, so the number of revolutions = total distance / circumference.
keywords: total wire = sum of straight + curved segments

key_terms.Sector: The region of a circle enclosed by two radii and the arc between them.
key_terms.Segment: The region between a chord and the arc it cuts off.
key_terms.Minor sector/segment: The smaller of the two regions formed.
key_terms.Major sector/segment: The larger of the two regions formed.
key_terms.Arc length: The length of the curved boundary of a sector.

important_facts: Circumference = 2*pi*r; Area = pi*r^2.
Sector area = (theta/360)*pi*r^2; arc length = (theta/360)*2*pi*r.
Segment area = sector area - triangle area (for the minor segment).
Equilateral triangle inscribed in a circle of radius R: side = R*sqrt(3), altitude = (3/2)*R.
Number of revolutions to cover a distance = total distance / circumference.
exam_tips: For 'remaining/shaded area' questions, write out the full-figure area and each individual cut-out area separately before combining them - trying to do it all in one step is where sign errors creep in.
Use pi=22/7 when the radius is a multiple of 7 (it usually cancels cleanly); otherwise pi=3.14 is often intended.

When a problem mentions several identical circles arranged inside a square or rectangle, sketch a quick grid to work out how the side length of the outer figure relates to the circles' diameters before calculating.

questions.question: The circumference of a circle of radius 7 cm is: (use pi = 22/7)
questions.explanation: Circumference = 2*pi*r = 2*(22/7)*7 = 44 cm.

questions.question: The area of a circle of radius 14 cm is: (use pi = 22/7)
The area of a sector of a circle with radius 21 cm and sector angle 60 degrees is: (use pi = 22/7)

questions.explanation: Altitude of an equilateral triangle inscribed in a circle of radius R is (3/2)*R = (3/2)*6 = 9 cm.

questions.question: The largest circle that can be drawn inside a square of side 14 cm has an area of: (use pi = 22/7)
questions.explanation: The largest inscribed circle has diameter equal to the square's side, so radius = 7 cm. Area = (22/7)*7^2 = 154 cm2.

questions.question: A wheel of radius 0.25 m rolls without slipping. The distance it covers in one revolution is: (use pi = 22/7)
questions.explanation: Distance in one revolution = circumference = 2*(22/7)*0.25 = 11/7 approx 1.57 m.

questions.question: Find the area and arc length of a sector of radius 7 cm with a central angle of 90 degrees. (use pi = 22/7)
Find the area of the remaining portion of a square of side 14 cm after the largest possible circle is cut out from it. (use pi = 22/7)

rubric.point: Square area = 14^2 = 196 cm2; inscribed circle radius = 7 cm, area = 154 cm2

questions.model_answer: Square area = 14x14 = 196 cm2. The largest inscribed circle has radius 7 cm, area = (22/7)x7^2 = 154 cm2. Remaining area = 196-154 = 42 cm2.

questions.question: Find the area of the minor segment of a circle of radius 14 cm, cut off by a chord that subtends a right angle (90 degrees) at the centre. (use pi = 22/7)

rubric.point: Triangle area (right angle, legs = radius = 14) = (1/2)*14*14 = 98 cm2

questions.model_answer: Sector area = (90/360)*(22/7)*14^2 = (1/4)*616 = 154 cm2. The triangle formed by the two radii and chord is right-angled with both legs equal to the radius (14 cm), so its area = (1/2)*14*14 = 98 cm2. Segment area = sector area - triangle area = 154-98 = 56 cm2.

questions.question: Four circles, each of radius 7 cm, are drawn touching each other inside a square. Find the area of the square and the area of the space left over after cutting out the four circles. (use pi = 22/7)

rubric.point: Square side = 2 x (2x7) = 28 cm (a 2x2 arrangement of circles of diameter 14 each)
Square area = 28^2 = 784 cm2; total circle area = 4 x (22/7) x 7^2 = 4x154=616 cm2

questions.model_answer: With four circles of radius 7 cm (diameter 14 cm) arranged in a 2x2 grid, the square's side = 2x14 = 28 cm. Square area = 28^2 = 784 cm2. Each circle's area = (22/7)x7^2 = 154 cm2, so total circle area = 4x154 = 616 cm2. Remaining area = 784-616 = 168 cm2.

questions.topic: Comprehensive - sector, segment and shaded region
questions.question: A chord of a circle of radius 10 cm subtends a right angle at the centre. Find (a) the area of the minor sector, (b) the area of the minor segment, (c) the area of the major segment. (use pi = 3.14)
questions.model_answer: (a) Minor sector area = (90/360)*3.14*10^2 = 78.5 cm2. (b) The triangle formed by the two radii and chord is right-angled with legs 10 cm each, area = (1/2)x10x10 = 50 cm2. Minor segment area = 78.5-50 = 28.5 cm2. (c) Total circle area = 3.14x100 = 314 cm2. Major segment area = total circle area - minor segment area = 314-28.5 = 285.5 cm2.

questions.topic: Case study - Pookalam flower-bed design (adapted from CBSE Question Bank)
questions.passage: During Onam, a school is planning a Pookalam (flower-bed pattern) competition. Design I is made with a circle of radius 32 cm, with an equilateral triangle ABC inscribed inside it. Design II is made with 9 identical circular designs, each of radius 7 cm, arranged in a 3x3 grid inside a square.

subquestions.question: Referring to Design I, what is the altitude of the inscribed equilateral triangle?
subquestions.explanation: Altitude of an equilateral triangle inscribed in a circle of radius R is (3/2)*R = (3/2)*32 = 48 cm.

subquestions.question: Referring to Design II, what is the area of the square that exactly contains the 3x3 grid of circles (each of radius 7 cm)?
subquestions.explanation: Each circle has diameter 14 cm, and 3 circles fit across each side, so the square's side = 3x14 = 42 cm. Area = 42^2 = 1764 cm2.

subquestions.question: Find the area of the remaining portion of the square in Design II, after the 9 circles are removed. (use pi = 22/7) Show your working.

rubric.point: Area of each circle = (22/7)x7^2 = 154 cm2, so 9 circles = 9x154 = 1386 cm2

subquestions.model_answer: Area of each circle = (22/7)x7^2 = 154 cm2, so 9 circles have total area 9x154 = 1386 cm2. Remaining area = square area - total circle area = 1764-1386 = 378 cm2.

questions.topic: Case study - designing a brooch (adapted from CBSE Question Bank)
questions.passage: A brooch is a small piece of jewellery with a pin at the back so it can be fastened on a dress or coat. One design (Design A) is made with silver wire in the form of a circle of diameter 28 mm, with 4 diameters drawn across it dividing the circle into 8 equal sectors.

subquestions.question: What is the total length of silver wire required for Design A (the circle plus the 4 diameters)? (use pi = 22/7)
subquestions.explanation: Circumference = (22/7)x28 = 88 mm. The 4 diameters add 4x28=112 mm of wire. Total = 88+112 = 200 mm.

subquestions.question: What is the area of each of the 8 equal sectors in Design A? (use pi = 22/7)
subquestions.explanation: Circle area = (22/7)x14^2 = 616 mm2. Each of the 8 equal sectors has area 616/8 = 77 mm2.

subquestions.question: In a second design (Design B), the gold outer band has an outer radius of 10 mm. If a boy rolls the brooch along its edge, how many complete revolutions does it take to cover a distance of 80*pi mm? Show your working.
subquestions.model_answer: Circumference of the outer edge = 2*pi*10 = 20*pi mm. Number of revolutions to cover 80*pi mm = (80*pi)/(20*pi) = 4.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The area of a sector with angle 180 degrees is exactly half the area of the full circle.
Reason (R): Sector area = (theta/360)*pi*r^2, and substituting theta=180 gives exactly half of pi*r^2.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: A is true (a 180-degree sector is a semicircle, exactly half the circle). R correctly derives this from the sector area formula.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): An equilateral triangle inscribed in a circle of radius 10 cm has side length 10*sqrt(3) cm.
Reason (R): For an equilateral triangle inscribed in a circle of radius R, side = R*sqrt(3).
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Both A and R are true, and applying the formula in R directly gives the value in A (10*sqrt(3)).

questions.question: The angle swept by the minute hand of a clock in 15 minutes is:
questions.explanation: The minute hand sweeps 360 degrees in 60 minutes, so in 15 minutes it sweeps (15/60)*360 = 90 degrees.

A wheel of radius 0.7 m covers 44 m. The number of revolutions it makes is: (use pi=22/7)
questions.explanation: Circumference = 2*(22/7)*0.7 = 4.4 m. Revolutions = 44/4.4 = 10.

questions.question: The perimeter of a semicircle of radius 7 cm is: (use pi=22/7)
questions.explanation: Perimeter of a semicircle = pi*r+2r = 22+14 = 36 cm.

questions.question: Find the area of a sector of radius 7 cm with a central angle of 30 degrees. (use pi=22/7)
The circumference of a circle is 88 cm. Find its area. (use pi=22/7)
questions.model_answer: r = circumference/(2*pi) = 88/(2x22/7) = 14 cm. Area = (22/7)x14^2 = 616 cm2.

questions.question: Find the area of a quadrant of a circle whose radius is 7 cm. (use pi=22/7)
A wheel has a radius of 35 cm. Find the distance covered (in km) in 1000 revolutions. (use pi=22/7)
questions.model_answer: Circumference = 2*(22/7)*35 = 220 cm. Distance in 1000 revolutions = 1000x220 = 220000 cm = 2.2 km.

questions.question: Find the perimeter of a sector of radius 5.6 cm with a central angle of 60 degrees. (use pi=22/7)
questions.model_answer: Arc length = (60/360)*2*(22/7)*5.6 = (1/6)*35.2 approx 5.87 cm. Perimeter = arc + 2r = 5.87+11.2 approx 17.07 cm.

questions.question: The minute hand of a clock is 14 cm long. Find the area swept by it in 5 minutes. (use pi=22/7)
questions.model_answer: In 5 minutes, the minute hand sweeps (5/60)*360 = 30 degrees. Area swept = (30/360)*(22/7)*14^2 = (1/12)*616 approx 51.33 cm2.

questions.question: Find the radius of a circle whose circumference is equal to the sum of the circumferences of two circles with radii 19 cm and 9 cm.

rubric.point: Since circumference is proportional to radius, the radii simply add: r=19+9

questions.model_answer: Circumference = 2*pi*r, so if the new circle's circumference equals the sum of the two given circumferences, then 2*pi*r = 2*pi*19+2*pi*9, giving r=19+9=28 cm.

questions.question: Find the area and the arc length of a sector of radius 21 cm with a central angle of 60 degrees. (use pi=22/7)
A circle of the largest possible size is cut from a square sheet of side 14 cm. Find the area of the circle and the area of the leftover material.

rubric.point: Radius of inscribed circle = 7 cm (half the side)
Leftover = square area - circle area = 196-154 = 42 cm2

questions.model_answer: The largest circle that fits in a 14x14 square has radius 7 cm (half the side). Circle area = (22/7)x49 = 154 cm2. Square area = 14x14 = 196 cm2. Leftover material = 196-154 = 42 cm2.

questions.question: A sector of a circle of radius 21 cm has a central angle of 60 degrees. Find (a) the area of the sector, (b) the length of the arc, (c) the area of the corresponding minor segment. (use pi=22/7, sqrt(3)=1.732)

rubric.point: (c) The triangle formed (two radii plus chord, 60 degree apex) is equilateral with side 21
(c) Segment area = sector - triangle approx 231-190.96 = 40.04 cm2

questions.model_answer: (a) Sector area = (60/360)*(22/7)*441 = 231 cm2. (b) Arc length = (60/360)*2*(22/7)*21 = 22 cm. (c) Since the central angle is 60 degrees and both radii equal 21 cm, the triangle formed is equilateral with side 21 cm. Its area = (sqrt(3)/4)*21^2 = (1.732/4)*441 approx 190.96 cm2. Segment area = sector area - triangle area = 231-190.96 approx 40.04 cm2.

questions.topic: Comprehensive - circle inscribed in square, remaining area
questions.question: A square plot of side 14 m has the largest possible circular flower bed cut into it. Find (a) the area of the circular flower bed, (b) the area of the square plot, (c) the area of the remaining plot (outside the circle), and (d) what percentage of the square's area the flower bed occupies (to 1 decimal place). (use pi=22/7)
questions.model_answer: (a) The largest circle fitting in the square has radius 7m (half the side), area = (22/7)x49 = 154 sq m. (b) Square area = 14x14 = 196 sq m. (c) Remaining area = 196-154 = 42 sq m. (d) Percentage occupied by the flower bed = (154/196)x100 approx 78.6%.

questions.topic: Perimeter of a sector-shaped model given its area and angle
questions.question: Wasim made a Pac-Man-shaped model with an area of 120*pi sq cm, where the 'mouth' cut out of the circle forms an angle of 60 degrees at the centre (i.e. the model is the remaining 300-degree sector). He wants to attach a ribbon around the entire boundary of the shape (the curved arc plus the two straight edges of the mouth). What is the minimum length of ribbon required, in terms of pi?

rubric.point: Area of the 300-degree sector = (300/360) x pi x r^2 = 120pi, solving gives r = 12 cm
Boundary = arc length + 2 straight radii = (300/360) x 2 x pi x 12 + 2(12) = 20pi + 24 cm

questions.model_answer: Let the radius be r cm. The area of the 300-degree sector (full circle minus the 60-degree mouth) is (300/360) x pi x r^2 = 120pi, which gives r^2 = 144, so r = 12 cm. The boundary of the shape consists of the curved arc plus the two straight edges of the mouth (each of length r): arc length = (300/360) x 2 x pi x 12 = 20pi cm, plus 2 x 12 = 24 cm for the two straight edges. Total ribbon required = (20pi + 24) cm.

questions.topic: Case study - sector and triangle areas in a trophy shield
questions.passage: Akshi received a trophy shield made of a glass sector DOC, supported on either side by two identical wooden right-angled triangles, triangle DAO and triangle COB, each right-angled at A and B respectively (so OA and OB are the straight base edges, and D, C are the outer corners of the wooden triangles touching the circular sector). AO = 7 cm, and AO : DA = 1 : sqrt(3) (use sqrt(3) = 1.73).

subquestions.question: Find angle DOC (the angle of the glass sector at the centre O).

rubric.point: In right triangle DAO, tan(angle DOA) = DA/AO = sqrt(3), so angle DOA = 60 degrees; by symmetry angle COB = 60 degrees too, so angle DOC = 180 - 60 - 60 = 60 degrees

subquestions.model_answer: In right triangle DAO (right-angled at A), tan(angle DOA) = DA/AO = sqrt(3), so angle DOA = 60 degrees. By the symmetric construction, angle COB = 60 degrees as well. Since D, O, C, A, B lie so that angle DOA + angle DOC + angle COB = 180 degrees (a straight line through O), angle DOC = 180 - 60 - 60 = 60 degrees.

subquestions.question: Find the combined area of the two wooden right-angled triangles.

rubric.point: DA = AO x sqrt(3) = 7 x 1.73 = 12.11 cm; area of one triangle = (1/2)(AO)(DA) = (1/2)(7)(12.11) = 42.385 cm^2; two identical triangles give 2 x 42.385 = 84.77 cm^2

subquestions.model_answer: DA = AO x tan(60) = 7 x sqrt(3) = 7 x 1.73 = 12.11 cm. Area of one right triangle = (1/2) x AO x DA = (1/2)(7)(12.11) = 42.385 cm^2. Since both wooden triangles are identical, their combined area = 2 x 42.385 = 84.77 cm^2.

subquestions.question: Find the area of the glass portion (the sector DOC).

rubric.point: DO (hypotenuse of triangle DAO) = AO/cos(60) = 7/0.5 = 14 cm - this is the radius of sector DOC
Area of sector DOC = (60/360) x pi x 14^2 = 102.67 cm^2 (using pi = 22/7)

subquestions.model_answer: In right triangle DAO, DO = AO/cos(60 degrees) = 7/0.5 = 14 cm, which is the radius of the glass sector DOC. The area of the 60-degree sector DOC = (60/360) x pi x (14)^2 = (1/6) x (22/7) x 196 = 102.67 cm^2.
